headline: Low-income college students relied on campus child care. Then Trump cut it.
author: Danielle Douglas-Gabriel

paragraphs.text: At the start of this semester, Larissa Saucillo was making great progress toward becoming a nurse.

Saucillo, 33, got into two popular evening lab courses that accommodated her full-time work schedule. And she secured a slot for her 5-year-old daughter in the college’s evening child care program, a service backed by a federal grant for low-income college students with children.

But a month into the current term, Saucillo learned the federal grant had run out, and the community college’s program was inexplicably denied new funding. Without child care, there was no way Saucillo could continue her classes, so she withdrew.

“It’s going to take me at least another semester now to complete my program,” Saucillo said. “That means more student loans, more debt when I could have just gotten it done and moved on to the nursing program. That program is so competitive that I may not be able to get in until 2028.”

The Trump administration’s controversial decision to cut the number of colleges awarded funding from the Child Care Access Means Parents in School (CCAMPIS) program has forced some students to cut back their college courses or stop attending. The $75 million federal program offers four-year grants to colleges and universities that provide child care on campus or in the surrounding community. It is a critical source of money for public colleges that educate large populations of students with limited financial means, advocates and school officials said.

Despite announcing plans this summer to provide 148 colleges with CCAMPIS funding through a new grant competition, the Education Department awarded only 40 grants in the fall. In its last grant competition in 2021, the department awarded funding to 327 colleges.

Advocates cried foul this fall after the Education Department gave all four years’ worth of funding to a few dozen colleges, instead of distributing the funding on a yearly basis to more schools from annual congressional appropriations.
The department typically avoids “front-loading,” but advocacy groups say the practice has become more common as the Trump administration tries to dismantle the Education Department.

Trump has twice proposed eliminating CCAMPIS, claiming it is misaligned with the Education Department’s purpose and would be best run by the Department of Health and Human Services. The administration off-loaded the child care program to HHS last year through an interagency agreement that left the Education Department in a supervisory role.
The Education Department did not explain the discrepancy between the anticipated and actual number of CCAMPIS awards, but said its decision is in line with the administration’s policy objectives.

“ED is forward funding successful applicants where the administration has not requested funding in future budget years to avoid interrupting projects partway into their project period,” Education Department spokesperson Ellen Keast said in an email. “We are ending the failed approach of previous administrations and funding high-quality grantees.”

Advocates argue there was no shortage of colleges offering high-quality child care. The department received nearly 300 applications, and public records show that 79 applicants earned perfect scores on their proposals. Yet many of those colleges were shut out of the awards.

Madison Area Technical College is one of them. The Wisconsin college, which has relied on CCAMPIS for the past eight years, received no explanation for the rejection, just glowing feedback from application reviewers. It had requested a little over the $2 million the college received in 2021.

Madison has two campus-based child care centers and has increased capacity three times since 2020 from 30 children to more than 120 children, as more students need a safe, convenient and affordable place to leave their children during class. Roughly 40 percent of full-time degree-seeking students at Madison are parents of young children.

With the loss of federal funding to subsidize the cost of care, six families have declined child care slots, three delayed starting care while seeking other funding, and two reduced their course loads to avoid the need for care in the past month, according to the college.

Madison President Jennifer Berne has been working with the college’s foundation to provide affected students temporary child care assistance, while rallying donors and the local government for additional financial support. But without federal funding, she said there is no way to guarantee the college can support parents through the completion of their education.

“This is a workforce issue,” Berne said. “We have the talent and motivation of the people who want to become nurses, mechanics, accountants … but without child care, they cannot access those programs.”

For college students with children — roughly 1 in 5 undergraduates — reliable and affordable child care can make or break their chances of earning a credential. In a 2024 survey conducted by the think tank New America, more than half of parenting community college students who dropped out said affordable child care would help them return to college. Only 38 percent of community colleges offer on-campus child care.

Demand for child care slots at many campuses has historically outpaced supply, leading to lengthy wait lists that have caught the attention of federal lawmakers. Congress increased CCAMPIS funding from $15 million to $75 million between 2017 and 2023, allowing more colleges and universities to access federal support. Still, the funding has never been enough to meet the full need.

When Madison lost its federal funding, graphic design student Christopher Rothe, 40, could no longer afford to send his 20-month-old son to the campus center five days a week. His boy now goes three days a week and spends the other two with Rothe, who had to cut back on his hours at work and his course load to stay home with his son.

“I’m really trying to get us to a point of being financially secure, into a better apartment, you know, just creating a better life for our family,” Rothe said. “I don’t know how long it’s going to take to finish my program now that I have to take fewer classes.”

In a letter sent earlier this month to Education Secretary Linda McMahon, Sens. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) and Patty Murray (D-Washington), high-ranking members of the Appropriations Committee, criticized the Education Department’s treatment of CCAMPIS and other competitive grant programs that issued few awards and front-loaded congressional funding.

“It is perplexing that an administration that says it wants to improve affordability for Americans and help Americans find good-paying jobs would curtail a program that helps Americans afford higher education and workforce training,” the senators wrote.

Stephanie Baker, a senior policy manager in the higher education program at New America, said Congress could stipulate in the next appropriations bill that the Education Department hold another competition in 2027 for funding. Lawmakers, she said, could also direct the department to fund the slate of colleges that had strong applications but did not get grants.
But for now, colleges across the country are contending with the fallout of this year’s cut.

At Austin Community College, the $1.1 million in CCAMPIS funding from the previous competition has primarily been used to help students in its health science program, particularly those like Saucillo enrolled in night classes, said Cara Crowley, the special adviser to the chancellor for basic needs systems at the college.

She said the college began preparing students last year for the possibility that federal funding would not be renewed because there was so much uncertainty about the future of CCAMPIS under Trump. Some students qualified for a state grant that offset child care costs, but many others were left without any recourse.
ACC never received a response to its CCAMPIS application, and only learned that it was denied the federal funding after contacting Republican Sen. John Cornyn’s office in Texas.

About 30 percent of the 80,000 students at the community college are parents, and the wait list for child care slots has an average of 200 to 300 students every year. The college managed to reduce the wait list and open the nighttime program with its 2021 CCAMPIS award of just over $1 million, but now it is grappling with the loss of federal support.

Despite the setback, Saucillo remains resolute in becoming a nurse. She took a 75 percent pay cut to enroll full time and complete her program faster, but for now she can only take an online class without reliable child care.

“Everything is up in the air,” Saucillo said. “It’s unfortunate because I know I’m not the only parent going through this. We are all trying to provide better lives for our kids. … And the opportunity is being taken away.”
